title: How Much Land Does a Man Need?
text:
Pahom was a Russian peasant who said that if only he had enough land, he would not fear the Devil himself. The Devil heard him, and took him at his word.

Pahom bought a little land, then more. He moved to a bigger farm near the Volga and prospered, but it never felt like enough. Then a traveler told him about the Bashkirs, a people on the steppe who would sell their land cheaply. Pahom went to them. Their chief named a strange price: one thousand rubles a day. For that sum, Pahom could have all the land he could walk around between sunrise and sunset. But if he did not return to his starting point by sunset, he would lose his money.

At dawn Pahom set off with a spade, marking his corners as he went. The land was good everywhere, and he kept going a little farther to include one more meadow, one more hollow. By afternoon he realized he was very far from the start. He turned back and walked, then ran, his heart pounding, as the sun sank toward the horizon.

He reached the starting point just as the sun went down, and the Bashkirs cheered. But Pahom fell forward and lay dead. His servant took the spade and dug him a grave. Six feet from his head to his heels was all he needed.
lesson: Decide in advance what enough looks like. Without a limit you set yourself, every gain just becomes a reason to go a little farther than you can afford.
source: Leo Tolstoy, How Much Land Does a Man Need? (1886)
